findings.title: FlexiSPY is on this computer (installed application)
findings.description:
Covert monitoring software that captures messages, calls, location, and ambient audio, and is marketed explicitly for monitoring partners.

Found as installed application: /Applications/FlexiSPY.app.

This product is sold for watching another person without their knowledge. If nobody told you it was here, someone installed it to watch what you do on this computer.

Removing it can alert whoever installed it. If you think that's someone close to you, talk to an advocate before you touch it (US National Domestic Violence Hotline: 1-800-799-7233, or text START to 88788).

What to do: Don't remove it yet. Write down its name, where it was found and today's date, and make a safety plan first.

remediation.title: What to do about monitoring software

steps.title: Decide whether it's safe to remove
steps.body:
If you installed it yourself and use it (for example, remote support you
set up, or a parental-control app on your child's computer), you can stop here.

Otherwise, assume the person who installed it may notice when it stops
working. If that person is a partner, ex or family member, talk to a domestic
violence advocate before you remove anything; an advocate can help you plan
for what happens next. In the US: National Domestic Violence Hotline 1-800-799-7233,
or text START to 88788. Use a phone or computer the other person can't reach.

Workplace monitoring is made for an employer recording activity on work
computers; parental controls are made for a parent watching a child's
messages, browsing and screen time. To tell which this is: if you're worried
someone is watching you, treat it as monitoring software someone put here
without asking: don't remove it yet, and write down what was found and when.
If this is a work computer and you aren't worried, it's most likely there for
work; your IT department can tell you. If this computer is a child's and a
parent set it up, it's most likely that. Work software on your own computer
is worth asking about: what it records, when, and who sees it. The rules
differ from place to place; a workers' rights group or legal aid can tell you
what's allowed where you live.

steps.title: Keep a record
steps.body:
On paper or on another device, write down the name the scan found, where it
was found, and today's date. Take a photo of the scan result with your phone.
That record can matter later, for a protective order or a police report, and
removing the software erases most of it.

steps.title: Secure your accounts from a different device
steps.body:
Monitoring software can see what you type on this computer, including new
passwords. Using a phone or computer the other person has never had access to:

1. Change the password for your email first, then your Apple Account or
   Microsoft account, then banking and social media.
2. Turn on two-step sign-in for each of them.
3. Sign out of every other session (most services have "Sign out of all
   devices" in their security settings).

steps.title: Remove it when it's safe
steps.body:
1. Use the program's own uninstaller if it has one. Deleting only the files you
   can see often leaves a background copy that puts it back.
2. Run the checkup again. These products often install a background service
   and a startup item as well; the new scan shows anything left behind.
3. On a Mac, also look in System Settings > General > Login Items & Extensions,
   and in System Settings > Privacy & Security under Accessibility, Screen
   Recording and Input Monitoring, and turn off anything you don't recognize.
4. On Windows, also look in Task Manager > Startup apps.

steps.title: Consider a fresh start
steps.body:
The most reliable way to be sure monitoring software is gone is to back up
your documents and photos (not apps), erase the computer and reinstall the
operating system. Think about this if anything still feels wrong after
removal, or if you can't tell what else was changed.

findings.title: Unrecognized apps have keyboard access: com.example.keys
findings.description:
1 app has permission to see your keyboard input, but we don't recognize them: com.example.keys. Many normal tools (like keyboard remappers or game launchers) ask for this, so it is not automatically a sign of spying. However, if you do not remember installing one, it is worth checking.

If you think someone close to you set this up to monitor you, removing it can alert them. Talk to an advocate first (US National Domestic Violence Hotline: 1-800-799-7233, or text START to 88788).

What to do: Go to System Settings > Privacy & Security > Input Monitoring. Turn off access for any app you don't recognize or didn't install yourself.

remediation.title: Investigate keylogger indicators

steps.title: Check unrecognized apps with keyboard access
steps.body:
Distinct from Step 2 — this is for apps that aren't on the known-keylogger
list but also aren't a recognized system app or common developer tool.

1. Look up the app's bundle identifier and name; check its install location
   (`/Applications`, `~/Applications`, or somewhere unusual like `/tmp` or
   `~/Library/Application Support`).
2. Search the exact bundle ID / name online for reports of it being
   adware, spyware, or a "stalkerware" product (these are often disguised as
   parental-control or "find my phone" apps).
3. If you can't establish it's legitimate, revoke its Input Monitoring
   access in System Settings > Privacy & Security, then quarantine the app
   the same way as Step 2 rather than deleting immediately.
4. If revoking access breaks functionality you actually rely on, that's a
   signal it may be legitimate — restore access and move on, but keep a
   note of what it was for future reference.

remediation.safety_note: Before you remove or turn anything off: if you think someone close to you set this up to watch you, removing it can alert them. Talk to an advocate first. In the US: National Domestic Violence Hotline, 1-800-799-7233, or text START to 88788.
